---
title: "Firebreak"
subtitle: "An AI SRE that investigates an incident, names a cause or says it cannot, and links every sentence to the query behind it."
---

## What it does

You give it a recording of an incident. It gives back one of two things:

- **A named root cause**, where every claim links to the query, time window and rows it came
  from.
- **An abstention**, which says nothing was unusual enough to investigate, and gives the number
  it measured and the threshold it compared against.

Before publishing, it re-runs every cited query. If a query now returns something different,
the claim that cited it is deleted.

## The problem it is built for

During an incident the hard part is not the fix. It is choosing which of forty services to look
at.

Two things make that choice hard:

1. **The service that alerts you is usually not the service that broke.** Payment fails, so
   checkout shows errors, so the frontend shows errors. The loudest service is the furthest from
   the cause.
2. **The reasoning disappears.** Whoever worked it out at 3am rarely writes down why, so the
   next person starts over.

An agent that answers faster helps with neither. A confident wrong answer sends people to the
wrong dashboard, and then they stop trusting the tool.

So Firebreak is built around two different questions:

- Can you **check** the answer?
- Will it **stay quiet** when the evidence does not support one?

## How one investigation works

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Incident recording] --> B[Statistics, no model]
  B --> C{Anything unusual?}
  C -->|No| D[Abstain and say why]
  C -->|Yes| E[Agent investigates]
  E --> F[Verify every claim]
  F -->|Claims hold| G[Report with citations]
  F -->|Too little support| D
```

Five steps, in order.

### 1. Load a frozen recording

An incident is stored as Parquet files, read through DuckDB. The same recording always produces
the same result, so when a number moves you know the code moved.

### 2. Run statistics first, with no model

Firebreak scores each service for how unusual it looks, then walks the service call graph to ask
which service best *explains* the pattern, rather than which one shows it most.

This runs before any model. It costs nothing and hands the model a shortlist of three services
instead of forty.

### 3. Stop here if nothing is wrong

If no service is unusual enough, the investigation ends. It reports the largest deviation it
found and the threshold that deviation failed.

On a healthy system, stopping is the correct answer.

### 4. Investigate, within a budget

A commander picks which theory to test next. Four specialists gather evidence, one each from
metrics, logs, traces and change history. A critic then argues against the leading theory using
the same evidence. Rounds, tool calls, tokens and elapsed time are all capped.

### 5. Verify, then publish

Six checks run on the finished report. The important one re-runs every cited query and compares a
hash of the rows. A claim that fails is removed rather than flagged, because a flagged claim
still gets quoted.

## How well does it work

Not measured yet, and this page will not show a number it cannot support.

The evaluation harness is built, and it currently reports that it has nothing publishable. That
is the harness doing its job. `reports/eval/` holds eight reports, each marked
`quotable_as_a_result: false` with a reason, and the build will not publish a figure from any of
them.

Two things are missing, and neither is a coding task:

| Missing | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Model credentials | No model has run, so there is nothing yet to measure about model quality |
| Recordings for the held-out splits | The library is {{< var specs >}} specs; only one tuning split is partly recorded |

Once both exist, `make eval` and `make site-stats` fill in every figure here automatically. See
[what is next](next.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## The one number worth knowing now

The same statistics step scores very differently on generated test data and on real recordings:
nearly every fault on generated data, and {{< var recorded_root_cause_correct >}} of
{{< var recorded_root_cause_applicable >}} on real recordings.

Generated data is not an easier version of real data. It is a different difficulty altogether.
That gap is the most useful thing this project has measured, and it is why thresholds tuned on
generated data are marked provisional everywhere they appear.
:::

## What is built

| | |
|---|---|
| Scenario library | {{< var specs >}} fault-injection specs across four splits |
| Offline demo | {{< var showcase_incidents >}} incidents replayed from {{< var showcase_cassettes >}} saved answers, with no model or network |
| Tools | 14, each with a fixed query shape, a row cap, and its own provenance record |
| Decision records | {{< var adrs >}}, each listing what it rejected |
| Tests | {{< var tests_passed >}} passing, {{< var coverage_percent >}}% coverage |

Every number above is generated from a file in `reports/`. No page here types a figure by hand.

## Try it

No model, no Docker, no network.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hoomanesteki/firebreak-ai-sre-agent.git
cd firebreak-ai-sre-agent
make setup
make demo
```

`make demo` rebuilds {{< var showcase_incidents >}} incidents from their specs and replays each
one. Two of them abstain, which is the correct answer for those two.

Then look at what an investigation produced:

```bash
make console   # http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The demo looks better than the real measurements

It replays saved answers from a deterministic stub, not a model, and it prints that before its
first line of output.

It names every fault in its set. The same statistics step, measured on real recordings, names
{{< var recorded_root_cause_correct >}} of {{< var recorded_root_cause_applicable >}}. The demo
shows the pipeline runs and reproduces. It says nothing about quality.
:::
